title: Sleep or journey
hook: Socrates, just sentenced to death: it is either a dreamless sleep or a journey, and neither is to be feared

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ecclesiastes, and your own voice first. Your line was what I think now. Did you get a few lines down? Keep them. Today, the first teacher speaks. Day seven hundred sixty.

The vote has just been counted. An Athenian jury has sentenced an old man to death for corrupting the young and failing to honor the city's gods. A person might rage, or beg, or go silent. Socrates turns to the jurors who voted to acquit him and says, in effect: stay a minute, friends, let's talk while the officials are busy. And what he wants to talk about is the thing just handed to him. In Plato's account of the trial, the Apology, he lays out two possibilities for what death is, two doors, and walks through neither.
screen: `THE VERDICT IS IN.` → `STAY A MINUTE, FRIENDS.` → `TWO POSSIBILITIES.`

segments.voice: First, a silence he trusts. Socrates says he has an inner sign, a voice that all his life has stopped him when he was about to do something wrong, even in small things. That day, it never stopped him: not leaving home, not walking into court, not in his speech. He takes its silence as a hint that what is happening to him may be good. Second, the first door: sleep. Maybe death is nothing at all, no awareness, like a night of sleep without even a dream. Then he asks the jurors to think of their best night of deep sleep, and to set it against all the other days and nights of their lives. He says even the great king of Persia would find few days and nights better than that one. If death is like that, he says, it is a gain. Third, the second door: a journey. Maybe death is a move to another place, where the dead are. Then he would meet the poets and heroes of old and keep doing what he always did: asking questions, testing who is wise. And there, he jokes, they surely don't put you to death for asking. Fourth, either way. Socrates doesn't claim to know which door is real. His point is that neither gives a reason to be afraid. He tells them a good person has nothing evil to fear, in life or after death. And he ends: now it's time to go, I to die and you to live, and which of us goes to the better thing, only God knows. That is Plato's Socrates. Others in this block will answer differently, and will get their own day.
screen: `THE SIGN THAT STAYED SILENT.` · `DOOR ONE: A DREAMLESS SLEEP.` · `DOOR TWO: A JOURNEY.` · `NEITHER IS TO BE FEARED.` · then, large: `EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Take the first door. Think of the deepest sleep you can remember, the kind where you woke and no time seemed to have passed. Rest in that memory for a few breaths. Then take the second door. Think of a long trip, a new place, people you've wanted to meet, questions you'd ask them. Rest there for a few breaths. Then hold both at once, without choosing. Notice whether fear shows up in either one, and where. If this is tender for you today, rest in the breath instead. The bell holds the time.
Hypnos, Socrates's first picture of death in Plato's Apology: a sleep with no dream, no cause for fear. Today's word.
Your line: either way. Today, when a worry about an ending comes, try his move: name two ways it could go, and ask whether either one truly calls for fear. Day seven hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Students of philosophy read Socrates's closing words in Plato's Apology as an example of facing death with reasoning rather than fear, without claiming to know what death is.

fork.setup: you are Socrates. the jury has just sentenced you to death. the officials are busy. what do you do?
options: talk calmly with your friends about what death might be.
fork.reveal: he stays to talk, sets out two possibilities, and finds a reason to fear in neither.

original.note: Greek: hypnos, sleep. Socrates's first picture of death in the Apology is a sleep with no dream.

trapdoor: what you thought: Socrates was sure the soul lives on.
what it means: in the Apology he offers two possibilities, sleep or journey, and fears neither.
what a scholar hears: Apology 40a–42a, after the sentence; the more confident arguments for the soul come in a different dialogue, the Phaedo.

notes: Apology paraphrased throughout (Jowett 1871 is public domain but not on the validator's list).

Check the paraphrase details against the text: the sign's silence (40a–c), the dreamless night compared with all other days and nights and the Great King (40d–e), meeting the poets and heroes (41a–b), 'they do not put people to death there for asking questions' (41c), no evil to a good man (41d), 'I to die, and you to live' (42a).
Charges stated as corrupting the young and not honoring the city's gods (Apology 24b); kept brief.
Original: ὕπνος (hypnos). Confirm the transliterated pronunciation guide.
